title: Application of Microalloying for Controlling Recrystallization and Grain Growth During Downstream Steel Processing
abstract: Abstract Downstream processing of steel products involves a large variety of heat treatments in the ferrite as well as in the austenite phase. Different from austenite conditioning in the upstream processing stage, deformation and temperature schedules are usually decoupled in downstream processing. Fundamental characteristics of microalloying elements regarding their effects on recovery, recrystallization, phase transformation, and grain growth during downstream processing will be reviewed. Relevant characteristics of microalloying elements are the atom size, the solubility and temperature stability of related carbides or nitrides, the tendency of segregating at grain boundaries, dislocations and point defects, as well as the diffusivity. The various interactions and resulting microstructural effects will be demonstrated for several industrial steel developments. The selected examples cover microalloy effects in ferrite and austenite phases, under slow and fast thermal cycles, as well as during short and long heat treatment times. Based on the observations and the related interpretation, a qualitative understanding of the microalloy interactions will be developed that is generally applicable despite the considerable variation of processes and products. It will also be highlighted how appropriate process and microalloy adaptations resulted in remarkable product optimization under industrial conditions.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Thermomechanical processing (TMP) in its various forms is an essential and widely practiced methodology for producing modern high strength steels. TMP typically provides microstructures featuring small grain size, enhanced dislocation density, precipitate particles, and secondary hard phases. However, mechanisms such as recovery, recrystallization, grain growth as well as particle coarsening can cause microstructural softening, thus opposing the intended goal of TMP. Several decades of development work have resulted in elaborate industrial TMP practices controlling and limiting these adverse effects and are, accordingly, termed thermomechanical controlled processing (TMCP). Yet, even capable processing equipment might be confronted with temperature and deformation schedules being too challenging for reliably obtaining the desired microstructure and hence property spectrum under every-day industrial conditions. In this regard, dedicated alloy additions can assist to sufficiently extend the processing window, thus enabling reproducible and economic production  via  TMCP. [ 1 ]

Most powerful and consequently widely used in this context are the microalloying elements niobium, titanium, vanadium, as well as molybdenum. [ 2 ]  All four elements appear in the same neighborhood of the periodic table of elements (periods 4 and 5, groups 4 to 6) sharing physical and chemical similarities. [ 3 ]  Regarding TMCP of carbon steels, two characteristics are most important: (1) the capability of forming nitrides and carbides and (2) an atom size being considerably larger than that of iron. [ 4 ]  Titanium and niobium are the strongest carbide and nitride formers, while molybdenum does not tend forming such compounds in austenite. [ 3 ]  Hence, niobium and titanium have a comparably low solubility, typically not exceeding 0.1 mass pct even at high austenite temperature, whereas vanadium and molybdenum can be dissolved to a considerably larger amount. On the other hand, the atom sizes of niobium, titanium, molybdenum, and vanadium are larger than that of iron, [ 5 , 6 ]  favoring their segregation at grain boundaries and dislocations. The binding energy of the atom to the austenite grain boundary, according to density functional theoretical (DFT) calculations, [ 7 ]  is by far highest for niobium, lower for molybdenum and titanium, and significantly lower for vanadium. The activation energy for static austenite recrystallization was found to be in linear relationship with the austenite grain-boundary binding energy, while the solute retardation parameter (SRP) exponentially increases with it. The SRP defines the time for the onset of recrystallization in the presence of the respective solute concentration in atomic percent relative to the time required by the unalloyed base material to recrystallize. Accordingly, the SRP is largest for solute niobium on a per atom basis. These more recent insights are implicitly reflected in the iconic diagram by Cuddy [ 8 ]  describing the effect of microalloy content on the temperature of non-recrystallization ( T NR ). Niobium clearly has the strongest effect on  T NR  per atom pct added. The fact that titanium, despite being a somewhat stronger carbide former and featuring a quicker precipitation rate, has a lower impact on  T NR  than niobium indeed suggests that the influence of solute drag must substantially contribute to suppressing recrystallization. It should be noted that precipitation of microalloys in hot austenite has a relatively slow rate following a C-curve behavior in a time–temperature diagram with the nose point being in the temperature range of 900 °C to 930 °C. Although deformation largely accelerates particle nucleation, neither Nb, Ti, nor V precipitate to completeness within the available time frame of industrial austenite conditioning processes. Even molybdenum, which is typically not precipitating in austenite, has been found producing substantial austenite pancaking, thus, solely based on solute drag. [ 9 ]  Using a semi-quantitative analysis, Hutchinson  et al . [ 10 ]  compared the effectiveness of niobium in impeding grain-boundary motion in solute and precipitate condition. It was concluded that the solute drag effect by niobium is more dominant in ferrite, whereas in austenite, NbC precipitate particles are assumed being more powerful. Maruyama  et al ., [ 11 ]  based on atom probe field-ion microscopy (APFIM), showed that the onset of austenite recovery in hot-deformed HSLA steels was retarded by solute atoms of microalloying elements with niobium having a larger retardation ability than titanium and vanadium. This is in agreement with the earlier cited density functional theory (DFT) calculations by Hoerner  et al . [ 7 ]  It was further claimed that not only single solute atoms but also Nb–N and Nb–C dipoles play an important role in the retardation of austenite recovery. Based on practical experience, it has been confirmed that under fast TMCP conditions,  e.g ., strip rolling with short interpass time, solute drag has a relatively more significant contribution to austenite conditioning, while precipitates may gain larger relevance in slower multi-pass processes like plate rolling. The vast body of data generated and the understanding developed over the almost six decades of research on microalloy effects in austenite conditioning have been implemented into various modeling tools. These enable reasonably accurate predictions of the microstructural evolution during austenite conditioning as well as assist in designing optimized TMCP schedules to achieve the desired microstructure.

Considering downstream thermomechanical processing, the impact of microalloying elements on recrystallization and grain coarsening phenomena is equally relevant but has been less consistently elaborated into modeling tools. The main reason is that microalloying elements, either appearing in solid solution or as precipitates, potentially interact at multiple stages over the wide range of downstream processes, often involving a larger complexity than that prevailing during austenite conditioning. In that respect, recovery, recrystallization, and grain coarsening can occur in the ferrite as well as in the austenite phase. Deformation processes are frequently decoupled from thermal treatments which quite often may even involve phase transformations. The duration of thermal cycles ranges from as short as a few seconds up to tens of hours, while heating and cooling rates can range from extremely fast to very slow. All these circumstances impact the constitution of microalloys either in solute or precipitate condition and may evoke significant  in-situ  alterations of their constitution.

In the following, several examples representing the complexity of downstream processing will be reviewed. Therefore, a principal understanding on how microalloying affects recovery, recrystallization, transformation, and grain growth mechanisms will be elaborated and substantiated by selected examples, representing cold-rolled automotive steels, line pipe steels, and case carburizing steels. All examples originate from research efforts within the market development programs of the Brazilian niobium miner CBMM (Companhia Brasileira de Metalurgia e Mineração) as well as the International Molybdenum Association (IMOA). Hence, the focus is primarily on the role of niobium and molybdenum, while other elements such as titanium, vanadium, aluminum, and boron will be discussed selectively to highlight similarities, differences, or complementary functionalities. The selected examples cover microalloy effects in ferrite and austenite phases, under slow and fast thermal cycles, as well as during short and long treatment times. Based on the observations and the related interpretation, a qualitative understanding of the microalloy interactions will be developed that is generally applicable, despite the considerable variation of processes and products. Appropriate process and microalloy adaptations that have resulted in remarkable product optimization under industrial conditions will be presented.

sections.heading: Annealing Treatments of Cold-Rolled Sheet Steel
paragraphs: The large variety of cold-rolled automotive strip steels is a consequence of the very different requirements in terms of strength and formability for producing individual components used in the car body. In order to achieve specific combinations of strength and formability, the microstructure must be adapted to consist of either single or multiple phases, including ferrite, pearlite, martensite, austenite, and bainite. This microstructural adjustment is always done in the final annealing process which can be batch annealing or continuous annealing, the latter most frequently being integrated in a continuous galvanizing line. The time–temperature schedule in the annealing process in combination with the cold reduction ratio (CRR) and the alloy concept determines the microstructural features and, thus, the properties of the finished steel.

The typical processing chain for the production of cold-rolled automotive sheet steel is schematically shown in Figure  1 . Hot rolling is usually finished at relatively high temperature without explicitly applying austenite conditioning. The coiling temperature is an important parameter that must be carefully considered (Figure  2 ). A high coiling temperature results in a ferritic–pearlitic microstructure and promotes precipitation of microalloying elements. The ferrite grain size becomes larger with increasing coiling temperature. A low coiling temperature results in the formation of non-polygonal ferrite and cementite particles. The precipitation of microalloying elements is substantially suppressed. Solute niobium produces an additional profound delay of transformation due to a drag effect on the phase interface. [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ] Fig. 1 Principal stages along the processing chain and temperature parameters for the production of cold-rolled automotive sheet steel grades Fig. 2 Schematic relationship between coiling temperature (CT) after hot strip rolling and solute microalloying element (MAE) content in ferrite. Influence of CT on precipitate particle size and ferrite grain size. Coiling strategy for eliminating (1) or maximizing. (2) MAE solute influence and optimizing precipitation strengthening in the hot strip

The precipitation kinetics of supersaturated niobium in ferrite has been investigated in detail by Perrard  et al . [ 15 ]  and is shown in Figure  3 . [ 16 ]  As expected, completeness of precipitation is achieved in a shorter time period at higher annealing temperature. Particle size increases with isothermal holding time and proceeds particularly rapid when annealing above the Curie temperature due to the significantly better diffusivity of niobium in paramagnetic ferrite. [ 17 ]  Furthermore, the NbC particle morphology shows an aspect ratio typically in the range of 2 to 2.5. [ 16 ]  A significant size difference between particles in steels with higher or lower niobium content under the same annealing conditions was not observed. Regarding Zener pinning, all these observations are relevant. For the same second-phase volume fraction, smaller particle sizes are more effective in pinning grain-boundary motion. Microalloy carbides (MC) establish a Baker–Nutting (B–N) relationship with a coherent interface along the habit plane [(100) α //(100) MC  and [010] α //[011] MC ] and an incoherent interface in the normal direction, resulting in a disk-shaped particle morphology. However, when transforming the ferrite host matrix into austenite, the orientation relationship at the prior coherent interface is broken. In that case, NbC particles attain a more spherical morphology and remain incoherent upon re-transformation to ferrite. [ 18 ]  Both features can have implications on the particle pinning potency. The pinning by coherent particles relies on both interfacial and misfit-generated elastic energies and can result in a more potent restraining effect on grain boundaries. This may enable stronger microstructural control relative to incoherent particles. [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]  Second, simulation of grain growth kinetics using the phase-field method revealed that second-phase particles with an elongated morphology are more effective in retarding grain growth. [ 22 ] Fig. 3 Kinetics of niobium precipitation out of supersaturated solution in ferrite (adapted from Perrard  et al . [ 16 ] ) in relationship to typical time–temperature conditions for coil cooling (from different coiling temperatures), batch annealing, and continuous annealing

The solute retardation effect changes when performing an annealing treatment in ferrite as microalloy precipitation proceeds  in-situ  with time (Figure  3 ). This mechanism is principally similar for all carbide forming microalloying elements. However, the precipitation kinetics is influenced by the formation energy, diffusivity, and particle misfit at the coherent interface for the respective microalloying elements. [ 29 ]  Molybdenum was often found to facilitate particle formation for all microalloy carbides, [ 29 , 30 ]  but still remains to a large extent in solution during such annealing treatments.

The constitution of niobium during the different industrial annealing cycles indicated in Figure  3  must be considered. The solute fraction of niobium existing at the onset of the annealing cycle is determined by the coiling condition according to Figure  3  or by an optional intermediate heat treatment before cold-rolling. [ 18 ]  In cycles executed at relatively low peak metal temperature (PMT) such as recovery annealing (1), niobium remains partially in solid solution. Recrystallization annealing (2) results in nearly complete precipitation. During intercritical annealing (3), used for producing advanced high strength steels (AHSS), a fraction of ferrite transforms into austenite. Transformation annealing (4) produces a normalized ferrite microstructure. It is worth noting that pre-existing (semi-)coherent precipitates principally cannot maintain their B–N orientation relationship upon recrystallization or transformation of the ferrite matrix. Different processing strategies with the resulting consequences for microstructure and properties will be discussed in the following sections.

sections.heading: Recrystallizing-Annealed HSLA Steel
paragraphs: Recrystallization in microalloyed cold-rolled steel is a complex process, as it involves a balance between the driving force for recrystallization and the retarding effect of microalloying elements, which can form precipitates. A fully recrystallized microstructure is often desired for improved ductility and formability. However, it can be challenging to achieve complete recrystallization during rapid annealing processes, such as continuous annealing. The resulting mechanical properties are a result of the interplay between recrystallization, grain size, and precipitation hardening. The Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) model [ 31 ]  can be used to describe the kinetics of recrystallization. Bleck  et al . [ 32 ]  investigated the influence of niobium microalloying on the recrystallization behavior in conventional HSLA steel. The temperature required for achieving a recrystallized fraction of 5 pct under isochronal annealing conditions linearly increases with the solute niobium content up to 0.05 mass pct by around 20 K per 100 ppm solute niobium. The effect is leveling off at higher niobium concentration. In a comparison with aluminum killed unalloyed steel, it was shown that a 0.04 mass pct Nb-steel needed around 80 times longer to develop 95 pct recrystallized microstructure at an annealing temperature of 700 °C. In a continuous annealing line, this necessarily requires raising the PMT toward 800 °C since the cycle time is typically limited to around 120 seconds. While a high degree of recrystallization is primarily restoring sufficient ductility to the cold-rolled steel, strength relies on a mix of mechanisms of which only solid solution strengthening is not affected by recrystallization. The contributions by grain refinement and precipitation, however, are majorly influenced by the pre-conditioning of the steel and the final annealing cycle. A low coiling temperature provides a finer hot strip microstructure and retains a larger fraction of microalloy in solution (Figure  2 ). The CRR determines the pancaking of the ferrite grains and the driving force for recrystallization. The degree of precipitation is controlled by the annealing temperature and time as well as the solubility product defined by microalloy and carbon content. [ 32 ]  The finer grain size resulting from a low coiling temperature reflects also in a finer grain size in the annealed product. Realistically, with the achievable minimum grain size of around 3  µ m in a recrystallized steel, the Hall–Petch contribution to yield strength is limited to around 180 MPa. In the range of applicable carbon and microalloy contents, full precipitation can add up to 220 MPa to yield strength. The base strength including solid solution strengthening is in the range of 130 to 150 MPa. Thus, maximizing all contributions would add up to a yield strength of 550 MPa. Practically, however, this scenario has no robustness in industrial production. Presently, recrystallized cold-rolled HSLA steel is supplied to the market up to a minimum yield strength of 500 MPa.

Automotive steel standards such as VDA239-100 specify the mechanical properties and their tolerable ranges. The allowable scattering range for yield strength is 90 to 120 MPa depending on the specified minimum yield strength from 340 to 550 MPa. It is not uncommon that a relevant number of coils falls outside the specified range in industrial mass production campaigns. A major root cause is the effective share of solute niobium in combination with the applied CRR and the annealing time-temperature condition potentially leading to varying shares of unrecrystallized ferrite. In this context, the coiling temperature and its possible variation over the hot strip coil length are often the origin of the problem. A practical remedy in that case is to increase the coiling temperature [scenario (1) in Figure  2 ], thus anticipating niobium precipitation and reducing the level of residual solute. This can enhance the robustness to property scattering but, on the other hand, reduces the strengthening potential by promoting ferrite grain growth as well as coarser-sized precipitates. For the steel grades in the range of 460 to 550 MPa, this approach might thus not be suitable, and one would better opt for scenario (2) in Figure  2 . In that case, it is important to coordinate the annealing condition (temperature-time) with the CRR (driving force) to prevent a high share of unrecrystallized ferrite.

sections.heading: Recovery-Annealed (‘Back Annealed’) HSLA Steel
paragraphs: The principle of the ‘back annealing’ method is to retain as much as possible dislocation hardening resulting from cold reduction while improving ductility through recovery and avoiding partial recrystallization. This is achieved by controlled annealing at relatively low temperature, also designated as back-annealing. An extensive review on the principles of back-annealing, its limitations, and the application to various alloy concepts was given by Ray  et al . [ 33 ]  Most importantly, the annealing condition must be defined such that under the given driving force (CRR), recrystallization is completely suppressed. Recovery involves a combination of mechanisms resulting in annihilation of point defects and dislocations, organization of free, random dislocations into dislocation walls or sub-boundaries, and coalescence of sub-boundary walls during subgrain growth. The formation of well-defined sub-grains often represents the first stage for nucleating recrystallization. However, the transition from recovery to recrystallization in ferrite can be rather diffuse and thus difficult to exactly determine. Whether a potential nucleus is becoming active will depend on its growth possibilities, particularly the presence of a growth-favorable boundary. Low-angle boundaries formed between sub-grains by recovery have low mobility, while boundaries with larger misorientations (> 10 to 15 deg) have high mobility. [ 34 ]  Consequently, a small fraction of sub-grains having a local misorientation of more than 15 deg can evolve into new rapidly growing grains eventually leading to a mixed microstructure consisting of pancaked recovered and abnormally large, recrystallized ferrite grains.

Simple carbon-manganese steels are not well suited for processing by back-annealing. Microalloying as typically used in HSLA steels enhances the robustness of the back-annealing process. The significantly different conditions between batch  vs . continuous annealing can be made comparable by using the Hollomon–Jaffe parameter ( H P  =  T  × [log(t) + 20] × 10 −3 , where  T  is the absolute temperature and  t  is the annealing duration in seconds). According to the data reviewed in, [ 33 ]  recovery occurs for  H P  values between 16 and 19.3, while full recrystallization and grain growth proceed when the  H P  value exceeds 20.5. The intermediate  H P  range (19.3 to 20.5) produces a partially recrystallized microstructure with a steep change in properties and is thus not suitable for robust processing in industrial production.

Based on the earlier described effect of solute drag on the mobility of dislocations and boundaries, the presence of solute niobium and molybdenum should have the best potential for widening the annealing window for stable recovery. Indeed, the effect of up to 0.09 mass pct Nb in retarding recovery and recrystallization during back-annealing has been demonstrated by Martin  et al . [ 34 ]  when producing cold-rolled HSLA steel with yield strength of 120 ksi (827 MPa) using a hot dip galvanizing line. From the production of interstitial-free (IF) steels, it is established that niobium-stabilized variants are finer-grained and thus stronger than titanium stabilized variants due to the higher resistance of the first against recrystallization. [ 32 ]  That result confirms the larger impact of solute niobium on the mobility of dislocations as compared to solute titanium. [ 25 ]

Using these insights, the possibilities for robust industrially producing advanced HSLA steels on either batch annealing (BA) or continuous annealing (CA) lines were investigated by Mohrbacher  et al . [ 35 ]  An extra-low-carbon (< 0.05 mass pct C) base alloy was microalloyed with 0.05 mass pct Nb (Nb-steel). A variant of that steel was additionally alloyed with 0.15 mass pct Mo (NbMo-steel). Hot rolling with high finishing temperature and subsequent coiling at low temperature (< 550 °C) retained a major share of the added niobium in solid solution. Some of the produced hot coils were batch annealed for 5 hours at 600 °C prior to cold-rolling. This intermediate heat treatment is expected to precipitate 50 to 60 pct of the available solute niobium according to Figure  3 . The comparison of the two conditions allows to verify whether solute or precipitated niobium is more effective in suppressing recrystallization. Two levels of driving force for recrystallization were adjusted, one by a low CRR, and the other doubling the CRR. The results obtained by the subsequent annealing treatments representing both, BA and CA lines, are summarized in Figure  4 . Under the annealing cycle of a BA line, both steel alloys rolled with low CRR remained stable in recovered condition up to an annealing parameter of 21.5. For the high CRR, the Nb-steel partially recrystallized already above an annealing parameter of 20.2, while the NbMo-steel resisted recrystallization up to an annealing parameter of 21.5. Thus, molybdenum provides an additional resistance to recrystallization even under a high driving force. The high CRR resulted in a strength increase of around 100 MPa in the recovered microstructure due to thinner ferrite pancakes developing a finer-sized substructure upon recovery annealing. Fig. 4 Property evolution along the processing chain and qualification of processing conditions for recovery-annealed HSLA steels (adapted from Mohrbacher  et al . [ 35 ] )

Under continuous annealing conditions, the Nb-steel with low CRR showed stability against recrystallization up to an annealing parameter of 22.2. Molybdenum alloying extended the limiting annealing parameter toward 22.5 and simultaneously provided a 50 to 70 MPa strength increase compared to the Nb-steel. The anticipated partial precipitation of niobium by intermediate annealing of the hot-rolled coil resulted in a lower strength of the Nb-steel under recovery annealing conditions. This is caused by coarsening of the ultrafine-grained (UFG) substructure [ 36 ]  probably due to the loss of solute niobium into precipitates and consequently enhanced dislocation mobility. The increased volume fraction of precipitates does not compensate the strength loss caused by substructural coarsening. On the contrary, pre-annealing of the NbMo-steel resulted in a strength increase after final recovery annealing. Solute molybdenum was capable of compensating the loss of solute niobium and thus prevented coarsening of the substructure. In that case, the anticipated NbC precipitation effectively contributed to enhancing the yield strength by 20 to 30 MPa. The average effective substructural grain size in the recovery-annealed steels was between 0.7 and 1.7  µ m, covering a yield strength contribution of 375 to 575 MPa according to the Hall–Petch relationship defined by Tsuchida  et al . [ 37 ]  for such ferrite–cementite microstructures. Precipitation strengthening adds 80 to 140 MPa and remained incomplete under these annealing conditions (Figure  5 ). Fig. 5 Strength contribution by NbC precipitates and grain refinement  vs . uniform elongation for different annealing conditions applied to cold-rolled Nb- and NbMo-steel (open symbols: as-coiled hot strip, filled symbols: pre-annealed hot strip) (adapted from Mohrbacher  et al . [ 35 ] )

sections.heading: Reverse Transformation-Annealed HSLA Steel
paragraphs: Some CA lines offer the possibility to anneal the strip close to or even above the  A c3  temperature. Such high PMT transforms most of the ferrite microstructure into austenite and back into ferrite upon down-cooling. This so-called reverse transformation annealing results in a normalization of the microstructure providing featuring equiaxed grain morphology and a high degree of isotropy. Precipitation of niobium can be considered being completed during the up-heating phase with the particles losing coherency by the reverse transformation. The effective grain size is the actual variable regarding the achievable strength by that process. To clarify this aspect, reverse transformation annealing trials were performed with the Nb- and NbMo-steels discussed in the previous section. [ 35 ]  The annealing temperature was set to 900 °C with the annealing parameter being above 25. The microstructure of the reverse transformation-annealed steels shows equiaxed ferrite grains with a normal size distribution around average values of 10 to 15  μ m. According to the Hall–Petch relationship, [ 38 ]  the yield strength contribution by grain refinement is in the order of 60 to 70 MPa. Little influence of the alloy composition and the pre-conditioning of the steel before cold-rolling was observed. The yield strength of all reverse-transformed steels was in within a narrow range of 350 to 450 MPa. The strength contributions and uniform elongation of the reverse transformation-annealed steels are compared to the recovery-annealed ones in Figure  5 . The reverse transformation-annealed steels achieve a maximum precipitation strengthening of 200 to 220 MPa. This is, however, too little to make up the loss in grain size strengthening seen in the recovery-annealed steels. The uniform elongation is rather stable on a lower plateau of ~ 8 after recovery annealing condition and on a higher plateau of ~ 20 pct after reverse transformation annealing, irrespective of the actual strength. On the contrary, partially recrystallized microstructures have a very strong variation of elongation with strength, making robust production in that annealing regime difficult.

Lesch  et al . [ 39 ]  proposed rapid transformation annealing (RTA) as a process combining high heating and cooling rates with a short holding time. Grain refinement after annealing of cold-rolled samples depends on the rate of recovery, recrystallization, transformation, and grain growth. [ 40 ]  Ideally, recrystallization is suppressed before transformation forcing austenite to nucleate from a pancaked ferrite microstructure. This mechanism is inverse to the widely practiced formation of fine-grained ferrite out of a pancaked austenite microstructure. Published results showed, however, that even when applying extremely high heating rates of up to 300 K/s, a fraction of ferrite grains recrystallizes. [ 39 , 40 ]  That recrystallized ferrite fraction is reduced by microalloying of niobium. The additional effect of molybdenum was not investigated in these studies. Karmakar  et al . [ 40 ]  highlighted the impact of the starting microstructure before cold-rolling on the recrystallization–transformation interaction. Accordingly, rapid recrystallization occurred in ferritic–pearlitic microstructure resulting in weak recrystallization–transformation interaction and, hence, in a coarser grain size after annealing. Strong recrystallization–transformation interaction with suppression of grain growth by uniformly distributed carbide particles was observed for a starting microstructure consisting of ferrite and fibrous martensite particles resulting in final ferrite grain sizes in the range of 1 to 6  µ m. However, it is unrealistic to produce such a precursor microstructure under industrial conditions. The more conservative RTA approach by Lesch  et al . [ 39 ]  requires high heating (> 40 K/s) and cooling (> 100 K/s) rates which are not achievable in commercially available continuous annealing or hot dip galvanizing lines, while the highest achievable yield strength would still remain below 550 MPa.

sections.heading: Intercritical-Annealed Steel
paragraphs: Dual-phase (DP) steel is widely used in today’s car body manufacturing. Considering their high strength, DP steels offer good global formability properties such as high strain hardening coefficient ( n -value) and total elongation (A80). However, DP steels are less capable in local forming operations involving bending, stretch flanging, or hole expansion due to the rather modest fracture strain. [ 41 , 42 ]  The inhomogeneous microstructure of soft ferrite and hard martensite in combination with localized straining is inherent to these problems. [ 43 ]  Advanced metallurgical concepts for DP steels aim to improve formability and damage resistance by modifying the microstructure through approaches like refining the overall grain structure, selectively strengthening the ferrite phase, and optimizing the spatial distribution of phases. [ 44 ,  45 ,  46 ,  47 ,  48 – 49 ]

The microstructure in DP steels during the intercritical annealing cycle is governed by the complex competition and interdependence of three primary mechanisms: recovery, recrystallization, and phase transformation. [ 50 ,  51 ,  52 – 53 ]  The outcome of this competition, largely controlled by annealing parameters, determines the final material properties. The interaction between ferrite recrystallization and austenite formation highly depends on processing parameters like heating rate and temperature. This interaction affects the morphology, size, and distribution of the resulting austenite (of which part transforms into martensite upon quenching) within the ferrite matrix. During the up-heating phase, recovery occurs first at lower temperatures or shorter times, reducing the dislocation density and stored strain energy through dislocation rearrangement and annihilation. Recrystallization follows recovery, leading to the nucleation and growth of new, strain-free ferrite grains, which significantly reduces hardness. Austenite then transforms into hard martensite during the final rapid quenching stage, forming the characteristic DP microstructure. The formation of austenite is influenced by the progress of ferrite recrystallization. The formation of new austenite can inhibit the recrystallization of ferrite. This is explained by the austenite providing a pinning pressure at the boundaries between deformed and recrystallized ferrite grains, slowing down or stopping further recrystallization. [ 51 ]  At lower intercritical temperatures, ferrite recrystallization dominates initially, leading to softening. At higher intercritical temperatures, austenite formation accelerates and dominates, leading to an increase in overall hardness after quenching due to the higher volume fraction of martensite. Ultimately, the degree of interaction between recrystallization and transformation results in the following microstructural characteristics:

Weak interaction (slow heating rate) At slow heating rates, ferrite recrystallization and cementite spheroidization are completed before the onset of austenite formation ( A c1  temperature). The austenite then nucleates preferentially at the junctions and boundaries of the newly formed, coarse, equiaxed ferrite grains. This results in a “necklace” morphology of austenite (which transforms into martensite upon fast cooling) along the ferrite grain boundaries, with large ferrite grain interiors. The larger ferrite grain size leads to slower austenite formation rates due to longer carbon diffusion paths.

Strong interaction (medium to fast heating rates) At high heating rates, ferrite recrystallization is delayed and overlaps significantly with austenite formation. The microstructure contains a mixture of unrecrystallized (deformed) and partially recrystallized ferrite grains. Austenite nucleates and grows rapidly along the dislocation-rich, deformed ferrite regions and prior pearlite colonies, which are typically aligned parallel to the rolling direction due to prior cold-rolling and often contain Mn segregation. The high dislocation density provides faster diffusion paths for solute atoms (like carbon). This leads to the formation of banded or elongated martensite islands parallel to the rolling direction within a non-uniform ferrite matrix. The presence of partially recrystallized grains can restrict austenite growth in the normal direction, leading to thinner bands at medium heating rates and thicker bands at faster heating rates (due to even less restriction).

In essence, controlling the degree of overlap between recrystallization and transformation domains through the thermal processing parameters (especially heating rate) is crucial for tailoring the final dual-phase microstructure and, consequently, the mechanical properties of the steel. The addition of niobium and molybdenum to DP steel with their individual and combined strong retardation of recrystallization during the up-heating cycle (as became evident form the previous sections) can decisively influence the overlap of these phenomena in favor of transformation and thus promote a strong interaction condition with resulting finer overall microstructures.

A typical time–temperature schedule for intercritical annealing in an industrial hot dip galvanizing line is shown in Figure  6 (a). An initial rapid heating in the direct flame furnace (DFF) section is followed by a much slower heating rate in the radiant tube heating (RTH) section up to PMT. This makes immediately obvious that the heating rate in the range of transformation temperatures is rather low. A detailed study of Bellavoine  et al . [ 54 ]  underlines that heating rates of at least 5 K/s are needed to reasonably retard ferrite recrystallization, while austenite formation kinetics has only limited sensitivity to the heating rate. An additional method to retard ferrite recrystallization is niobium and molybdenum microalloying which should make the effect of heating rate less critical. The progress of niobium precipitation was tracked at different stages of the intercritical annealing cycle in a low-carbon DP steel using a chemical extraction technique [Figure  6 (b)]. The results show that the fraction of niobium precipitates at the end of the fast up-heating stage in the DFF has only increased by around 10 pct over the initial as-hot-rolled condition. However, in the soaking zone, precipitation has reached a level of more than 90 pct. These observations are in good agreement with the precipitation kinetics shown in Figure  3 . The interaction of phase transformation and microalloy carbide precipitation has been described in detail by Gouné  et al . [ 55 ]  Accordingly, the transformation of ferrite into austenite allows the austenite to act as a carbon source for NbC precipitation in ferrite and also influences the driving force for precipitation. High concentration of solutes along the phase front could trigger a mechanism equivalent to the well-known interphase precipitation producing rows of very fine particles and high number density. This would make even small additions of niobium very effective as long as the majority of it is retained in solution by coiling at low temperature after hot rolling. Fig. 6 ( a ) Time–temperature schedule for intercritical annealing in a hot dip galvanizing line. ( b ) Progress of niobium precipitation analyzed by using a chemical extraction technique at different stages of the intercritical annealing cycle; HR: as-hot-rolled condition at low coiling temperature (Figure  2 ); DFF: end of direct flame furnace stage; RTH: end of radiant tube heating stage; Final: finish-annealed DP steel

Adding molybdenum to a 0.08 pct C to 2.0 pct Mn DP steel resulted in microstructural refinement. [ 49 ]  However, adding niobium to the same base alloy results in a more pronounced microstructural refinement. Molybdenum solely acts by solute drag which, however, weakens with increasing ferrite temperature and particularly above the Curie temperature (~ 770 °C) [ 5 , 6 , 17 ]  due to the enhanced diffusivity of alloying elements in the paramagnetic ferrite. [ 17 ]  Since niobium almost completely precipitates at such high temperatures [cf. Figure  6 (b)], it provides strong particle pinning contrary to molybdenum. The combination of the two alloying elements in the C–Mn–Mo–Nb steel produces a synergy of solute drag suppressing ferrite recrystallization at lower temperatures and subsequent pinning of ferrite and austenite grain boundaries by NbC precipitates in the intercritical temperature range.

Ramazani  et al . [ 56 ]  characterized the mechanical behavior of ultrafine-grained dual-phase microstructures. Remarkably and contrary to HSLA steel, the Hall–Petch coefficient for tensile strength is approximately twice as large as that for yield strength in DP steel. Bergström  et al . [ 43 ]  presented a dislocation-based theory explaining this effect in more detail. Consequently, grain refinement in dual-phase steel simultaneously improves strength, global formability properties related to strain hardening as well as local formability properties related to fracture strain. [ 46 , 48 , 57 ]

sections.heading: Re-Austenitized and Quenched Steel
paragraphs: The ultrahigh strength of press hardening steel (PHS) relies on reheating to fully austenitic microstructure and subsequent quenching in the stamping die, resulting in a martensitic microstructure (Figure  1 ). Austenitizing is typically performed at a temperature of 930 °C to 950 °C for a time period of 5 minutes. The prior austenite grain size (PAGS) is of considerable relevance for the properties of the final martensitic microstructure. [ 9 , 58 ]  Martensite transformed from a finer PAGS has superior toughness, [ 9 ]  increased fracture strain, [ 58 ]  and improved bending properties, [ 59 ]  which are all relevant to crash performance. Accordingly, austenite grain size control before quenching is a key aspect. The established PHS alloy concepts rely on boron and titanium microalloying. Solute boron by way of strongly segregating at the austenite grain boundary suppresses ferrite nucleation and greatly facilitates hardenability into martensite under cooling rates of > 30 K/s. The functionality of titanium microalloying is to bind residual nitrogen and thus prevent solute boron being consumed as BN precipitates. Typical titanium additions are over-stoichiometric to the nitrogen content (Ti:N > 3.4). Consequently, excess Ti is available for precipitation into TiC which should be useful for controlling grain size upon re-austenitizing in the hot stamping cycle. However, observations have indicated that titanium microalloyed PHS has insufficient resistance against austenite grain coarsening, especially when accidental overheating occurs, as demonstrated in Figure  7 . [ 60 , 61 ]  Since titanium carbide precipitates are known to be very stable at lower austenite and ferrite temperatures, the particle population must have changed while passing the intercritical temperature range during re-austenitizing. On the other hand, PHS with additional 0.05 mass pct niobium microalloying showed good grain coarsening resistance and a generally much finer PAGS (Figure  7 ). Fig. 7 Prior austenite grain structure of standard PH steel (22MnB5) and a variant microalloyed with 0.05 mass pct niobium after holding for 300 s at the indicated austenite temperatures (930 °C to 1030 °C) following a processing chain as indicated in Fig.  1  (adapted from Mohrbacher [ 9 ] )

Solubility products for microalloy carbides applicable to either austenite or ferrite are well established. [ 62 ,  63 – 64 ]  In full austenite phase, the nominal carbon content of the steel can be applied in the solubility product. However, in the intercritical ferrite phase, the carbon content varies as determined by the phase-field boundary Q–P–G in the binary iron–carbon diagram. [ 65 ]  Due to the diminishing carbon content in ferrite along the phase-field boundary segment P–G, microalloy carbide solubility remarkably increases in the intercritical temperature range [ 60 , 61 ]  becoming larger than that in the coexisting austenite phase. Taking the typical microalloy addition levels into account, titanium and especially vanadium carbide particles become partially or even fully soluble in the ferrite phase, whereas niobium carbide remains nearly insoluble even close to the  A 3  temperature. Therefore, it can be concluded that in the standard PHS, a share of the finer TiC precipitates redissolves in the intercritical temperature range leading to subsequent coarsening of surviving TiC particles. The NbC particle population however remains mostly stable. In dual microalloyed PH steel, the additional entropy of mixture of Ti–Nb carbide particles further enhances the resistance against redissolution in the intercritical temperature range. [ 60 ]  These observations are principally applicable to all microalloyed carbon steels being re-austenitized and might become even more relevant when applying slow heating rates.

sections.heading: Welding of Line Pipe Steels
paragraphs: Modern line pipe steels rely on a low-carbon content (≤ 0.07 pct) and medium to high niobium (0.05 to 0.10 pct) content. In that respect, they are very comparable to automotive HSLA steels. Adding suitable amounts of manganese, chromium, and molybdenum to such alloy concepts allows producing steel grades X70 and X80 with superior toughness properties. [ 66 ,  67 – 68 ]  Generally, the yield strength increases by 7 to 10 MPa per 0.01 mass pct of niobium added within a given alloy concept while simultaneously good toughness properties are maintained. [ 69 , 70 ]  However, it has been observed that toughness can deteriorate after welding in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGHAZ) when combining a high niobium with an extra-low-carbon content. [ 71 , 72 ]  The root cause of this deterioration appeared to be related to excessive grain coarsening in the CGHAZ. Near-stoichiometric titanium additions with respect to residual nitrogen are principally perceived beneficial with regard to CGHAZ toughness properties due to the dispersion of fine-sized TiN particles. These are stable even at highest austenite peak temperatures counteracting austenite coarsening by particle pinning. [ 73 ]  However, the use of this approach has not always been showing the desired success, while the targeted near-stoichiometric Ti:N ratio is difficult to consistently accomplish in industrial production. In a recent study, the influence of alloy concepts on weld zone microstructures and properties was systematically investigated. [ 72 ]  A HAZ simulator was used in that study homogeneously replicating heat cycles over a larger sample volume allowing to perform mechanical testing for specific subzones. For each of these subzones, the insights regarding the functionalities of microalloys gained in the previous chapter on automotive HSLA steels are fully applicable as will be demonstrated in the following.

sections.heading: Effect of Microalloying on HAZ Properties
paragraphs: Three principal alloy variants are considered, namely NbTi, MoNb, and MoNbTi allowing to identify individual and combined effects of these microalloying elements. In the considered base alloy concepts (see Table  I ), the niobium content is systematically increased from 0 to 0.1 mass pct. The steels were TMCP rolled after reheating at 1150 °C ± 10 °C and finished at 850 °C ± 20 °C followed by accelerated cooling to around 500 °C as described in Reference  72 . This processing resulted in an increasingly fine-grained acicular ferritic microstructure with rising niobium content. This microstructure contains a high dislocation density and is in that respect comparable to the condition of HSLA after cold-rolling. It is reasonable to assume that with increasing niobium content, an equivalent share remains solute after finish rolling, retarding the austenite-to-ferrite transformation toward lower temperatures. [ 12 , 14 , 74 ]  That fraction of solute niobium is available for  in-situ  precipitation during the weld cycle, again in analogy to annealing of automotive steel. Two thermal cycles simulating the heat input during welding were considered for analyzing the influence of niobium, molybdenum, and titanium on the recrystallization and grain coarsening behavior. Recovery and potentially recrystallization are expected to occur at the sub-critical temperatures due to the high dislocation density present in these steels. The intercritical weld cycle targeted a peak temperature of 900 °C, while the CGHAZ cycle applied 1350 °C. The heating time to peak temperature of 10 seconds and the down-cooling time from 800 °C to 500 °C ( t 8/5 ) of 25 seconds were identical in both cycles. Figure  8  shows representative microstructures of the NbTi steels treated by the intercritical cycle. The transformation points of all steel variants were determined by dilatometry (heating rate ~ 600 K/s). The lowest  A c1  temperature in these steels is 774 °C, and the lowest  A c3  temperature is 917 °C. Thus, with the chosen peak temperature of 900 °C for the intercritical thermal cycle, a substantial part of the microstructure is reverse-transformed resulting in a normalized grain structure. By repartitioning of carbon upon down-cooling, carbon-enriched austenite grains transform into martensite appearing as white contrast in Figure  8 . The non-reverse transforming ferrite grains are recrystallizing and grow to larger size accepting a polygonal morphology. Accordingly, the intercritical HAZ features a dual-phase microstructure with a low yield-to-tensile ratio (YTR). [ 72 ]  With increasing niobium content, the grain size in that zone is generally refined resulting in an increasing YTR and microhardness. [ 72 ]  The higher YTR allows concluding that less martensite is being formed in agreement with the microstructures shown in Figure  8 . While the microstructural evolution in the MoNb and MoNbTi steels is principally similar, molybdenum alloying enhances the share of hard phase. On the other hand, the grain size distribution becomes more homogeneous. Thus, molybdenum in combination with niobium appears to further obstruct ferrite grains growth during up-heating. The near-stoichiometric titanium addition, on the contrary, had no recognizable effect on the intercritical HAZ microstructure. Fig. 8 Light optical micrographs (etchant Le Pera) of comparing the simulated intercritical-annealed subzones of Ti-only and NbTi line pipe steels (adapted from Mohrbacher [ 72 ] )

The observed hardness increase of 30 to 60 HV over the range of niobium additions must majorly originate from  in-situ  NbC precipitation. Microstructural refinement and niobium precipitation result in a substantial increase of yield strength in the ICHAZ [Figure  9 (a)], while the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (T 50 pct ) decreases by as much as 40 K. Fig. 9 Ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (50 pct criterion) as function of subzone yield strength for the intercritical and coarse-grained heat-affected zone (adapted from Mohrbacher [ 72 ] )

These observations allow reconstructing the mechanisms acting on the microstructure during the up-heating cycle and which will be of decisive relevance for the development of the CGHAZ microstructure as follows: Niobium delays as-rolled ferrite recrystallization causing a strong interaction between recrystallization and transformation (as was discussed for DP steel in section II-D). Solute niobium precipitates as nano-sized carbide particles in the ferrite phase. The  in-situ  formed NbC precipitates together with pre-existing particles restrict the growth of re-transformed austenite grains by pinning. Molybdenum effectively complements niobium by additional solute drag on ferrite grain boundaries.

Figure  9 (b) presents the CGHAZ properties for the different alloy concepts. The yield strength increases with the niobium content and is comparably higher than that in the ICHAZ. The DBTT ( T 50 pct ) is significantly higher than in the ICHAZ, which in first place is related to the much coarser CGHAZ microstructure (Figure  10 ). The most essential observation is that the MoNb steels without titanium microalloying show very poor toughness performance, irrespective of the niobium addition. All Ti-free steels feature prior austenite grains with sizes larger than ASTM 4. On the other hand, all steels featuring lower DBTT (≤ − 30 °C) and a yield strength less than 480 MPa comprise a microstructure consisting of smaller PAGS as well as a significant share of ferrite plates. The presence of a finer-grained, interlocking ferrite microstructure, which is highly effective in impeding crack propagation, generally results in high impact toughness. [ 75 ]  The MoNbTi steel containing 0.05 mass pct Nb also featuring this microstructure (Figure  10 ) seems to be at the limit at which transition to low toughness occurs. The absence of ferrite plates in the CGHAZ of those steels showing inferior toughness performance could be the consequence of large PAGS in combination with delayed transformation influenced by the concentration of solute Nb and/or Mo at the boundary. Solute niobium originates from redissolution of precipitates in the CGHAZ. Gong  et al . [ 76 ]  quantitatively characterized the dissolution kinetics of niobium containing particles during isothermal holding at 1200 °C. The dissolution can be estimated as a function of time by using a modified JMAK equation. Wang  et al . [ 77 , 78 ]  demonstrated, based on weld cycle simulations with a MoNb steel, that redissolved niobium segregates strongly at the PAGB upon down-cooling from the peak metal temperature. Nb enrichment factors reached up to 3.50 at ferrite/martensite-to-austenite interface (FMAI) and 3.12 at PAGB. The pronounced Nb segregation at PAGB effectively inhibits austenite grain growth at high temperatures, while segregation at FMAI controls the growth of bainitic ferrite during cooling, leading to a finer, tougher structure. [ 78 ] Fig. 10 Light optical micrographs (etchant Nital) of the simulated coarse-grained subzone highlighting the effect of titanium microalloying (red arrows indicate prior austenite boundaries) (Color figure online)

The yield strength of the current low-toughness microstructures ranges from 480 to 530 MPa, regardless of the niobium content in the steel. This suggests that there is no significant re-precipitation of niobium at the low transformation temperature producing a microstructure mainly consisting of upper bainite and martensite–austenite (M–A) phase. On the other hand, in the steels comprising ferrite plates within the CGHAZ, niobium contributes up to 120 MPa (MoNbTi steel + 0.05 pct Nb) by precipitation strengthening which must be enabled by a higher transformation temperature of that phase. Garcin  et al . [ 79 ]  modeled the austenite decomposition in the CGHAZ for different thermal cycles. Principally, the observed phases in the present CGHAZ heat cycle simulations correspond to predictions by this model.

The present observations confirm that titanium is a key microalloying element for controlling the austenite grain size and, thus, the toughness properties in the CGHAZ. [ 73 ]  The experiments also indicate that a niobium content above 0.05 mass pct bears the risk of rapidly declining toughness properties. Bannerjee  et al. [ 80 ]  developed a model describing the non-isothermal austenite grain growth kinetics during thermal weld cycles. The model coupled kinetic aspects such as the mobility of austenite grain boundaries and thermodynamic aspects such as the dissolution of precipitates resulting the loss of pinning pressure. Under the assumption that abnormal grain growth does not occur, it was concluded that rapid dissolution of Nb-rich particles enables normal grain growth above the dissolution temperature. The model made reasonably accurate austenite grain size prediction being in the range of 30 to 40  µ m for heating rates of around 100 K/s to 1350 °C peak temperature in a low-carbon MoNbTi line pipe steel (0.034 mass pct Nb) steel. However, the large and sudden increase of transition temperature experienced by some of the steels presented in Figure  9 (b) must be caused by austenite grain sizes much larger than those expected by normal grain growth.

Abnormal austenite grain growth, specifically within the CGHAZ, is a phenomenon where individual austenite grains grow very rapidly to large size within a surrounding matrix that basically shows no grain growth. Welding simulations by Yu  et al . [ 81 ]  related the occurrence of this phenomenon to the quick dissolution of fine TiC precipitates above 1000 °C, while below that temperature grain growth was completely suppressed. Liu  et al . [ 82 ]  observed abnormal grain growth in the CGHAZ of Ti-only microalloyed HSLA steel when the Ti:N ratio was over-stoichiometric. The resulting coarser TiN particles were claimed to be less uniformly distributed providing insufficient grain-boundary pinning pressure. However, an over-stoichiometric Ti:N ratio will produce many fine TiC precipitates so that likely the explanation by Yu  et al ., [ 81 ]  namely the quick dissolution of TiC particles applied as well. In niobium microalloyed steels, this same mechanism based on quick dissolution of NbC precipitates should have the same consequences.

A theoretical consideration of the prerequisites and conditions leading to abnormal grain growth has been worked out by Rios. [ 83 ]  Accordingly, abnormal grain growth is likely to occur in a particle containing microstructure if the grain radius of the matrix equals a defined critical radius being related to the ratio of precipitate particle size to the particle volume fraction. An initially stable condition can turn to instability when particles start dissolving and ultimately disappear, thus when changing this ratio  in situ . A narrow grain size distribution is in that case the best remedy for preventing abnormal grain growth. Some of the features promoting abnormal grain growth may exist in the present steels: An initial bimodal grain size distribution after re-transformation to austenite with a fraction of extremely fine grains pinned by nano-sized NbC particles. Inhomogeneous concentration of niobium due to segregation during the solidification stage resulting in locally varying particle number density and thus pinning force. A fraction of precipitates having a low dissolution temperature and extremely quick dissolution kinetics due their very small size  [ 76 , 84 ] .

In contrast to ultrafine NbC particles losing stability in the temperature range of 1000 °C to 1050 °C, Nb, Ti (C,N), and TiN particles have a significantly better thermodynamic stability. [ 85 ]  Nb, Ti (C, N) mixed particles typically have a larger number density and more homogeneous spatial distribution than TiN particles which are often concentrated in segregation zones resulting a ribbon-pattern arrangement. [ 86 ]  Gong  et al . [ 76 ]  performed a quantitative analysis on the particle distribution and size after holding at 1200 °C for various time periods. The rate of coarsening was less in the NbTi-steel than in a Nb-steel because of the higher temperature stability of the (Ti, Nb) C or (Ti, Nb) (C, N) over the NbC or Nb (C, N) particles. On the other hand, TiN particles with an epitaxially grown NbC shell have no advantage in terms of particle pinning, whereas the involved share of niobium is withdrawn from producing smaller and better distributed Nb, Ti (C, N) particles. Participation of molybdenum does not significantly increase Nb, MoC particle stability at rather high austenite temperatures as can be concluded from the results of the Ti-free MoNb steels [Figure  9 (b)]. It should be noticed that the Ti-free variants may contain AlN particles, [ 35 ]  which dissolve at even lower austenite temperature (~ 950 °C) than NbC particles (~ 1050 °C).

Modeling work by Maalekian  et al . [ 87 ]  took a quick dissolution of fine-sized particles into account resulting in a significant decrease of the pinning pressure between 950 °C and 1050 °C. Abnormal grain growth can be triggered in such a case, especially when a sudden loss of pinning pressure occurs in a Nb-rich zone where simultaneously the preserved very fine austenite grain size induces a high driving force for grain growth. The more stable Nb, Ti (C, N) precipitates can counteract excessive austenite growth in the transient phase. Upon their complete dissolution, grain growth will be ultimately limited by insoluble TiN particles.

A laser ultrasonic measurement technique (LUMET) was utilized by Romualdi  et al . [ 88 , 89 ]  to  in situ  follow grain coarsening during weld heat cycle simulations. They investigated line pipe steels in the range of 0.03 to 0.07 mass pct carbon and 0.03 to 0.09 mass pct niobium. It was found that an increase in the amount of C and Nb in solution reduced the growth rate of austenite grains by solute drag. Additionally, molybdenum contributed to solute drag, be it to a smaller magnitude than carbon and niobium. The limiting austenite grain size, however, depended on the volume fraction and size distribution of Ti-rich insoluble particles. For the investigated steels, the final austenite grain sizes ranged between 40 and 120  µ m. A model based on these results allowed analyzing the relative effect of boundary pinning by insoluble particles  vs . solute drag on boundary mobility. Expectedly, solute drag became more relevant when the particle pinning pressure was low. Prerequisite for a strong solute drag effect is that the relevant atoms can accumulate to a sufficient concentration in the grain boundary. In that respect, the diffusion range of the relevant elements under the applied time-temperature condition as well as the migration rate of the boundaries must be taken into account.

Following Romualdi’s work, [ 88 , 89 ]  the solute drag potential of molybdenum could be the reason for the better performance of the MoNbTi steel with 0.05 mass pct Nb over the Mo-free variant [Figure  9 (b)]. Alternatively, molybdenum might enhance the thermodynamic stability of microalloy precipitates [ 90 ]  as will be discussed in more detail in  Section IV–B  of this paper. Commonly practiced moderate molybdenum addition (~ 0.2 mass pct) to NbTi line pipe steel was found to be beneficial in terms of balancing base metal strength and HAZ toughness performance. [ 91 , 92 ]  Excessive molybdenum addition, however, can cause an entirely bainitic microstructure in the CGHAZ along with an increased fraction of M–A constituents, both having a detrimental effect on toughness. [ 93 ]

sections.heading: Influence of the Carbon Content on the CGHAZ Microstructure
paragraphs: Raising the carbon level could be a possible approach to enhance the temperature stability of carbide particles. A detailed study on the influence of the carbon content in NbTi microalloyed line pipe steels on CGHAZ properties was reported by Ma  et al . [ 71 ]  Their results indeed indicated that raising the carbon content from 0.03 to 0.06 mass pct produced a smaller austenite grain size in the CGHAZ. The higher carbon content additionally decreased the austenite–bainite transformation temperature increasing the density and dispersion uniformity of high-angle misorientation boundaries which contributed to improved CGHAZ toughness properties. Romualdi’s work [ 89 ]  confirmed this by showing that the number of bainitic orientations within the decomposing parent austenite grain increased with the cooling rate due to a decreasing transformation-start temperature. A higher carbon content as well as an increased amount of solute niobium also reduced the transformation-start temperature provoking the same microstructural effect. The magnitude of the niobium effect is thereby controlled by its PAGB enrichment factor, which is influenced by non-equilibrium segregation during the down-cooling cycle. [ 77 ]

A recent study (not prior published by the author) on NbTi line pipe steels with varying carbon (0.04 and 0.06 mass pct) as well as niobium (0.06 and 0.10 mass pct) contents supports the findings by Ma  et al . [ 71 ]  The alloy compositions shown in Table  II  were produced by vacuum induction melting and subsequent split casting. In that way, the relevant alloying elements can be precisely adjusted, and the impurity level remains very low. The titanium addition was adjusted to a slightly over-stoichiometric Ti:N ratio (4.0 to 4.3),  i.e. , excess titanium is available for forming complex Nb, Ti (C, N) particles in austenite as well as ultrafine TiC precipitates in ferrite. The steel producers participating in this study deliberately apply this approach for maintaining a precipitation strengthening potential that can safeguard the minimum specified yield strength if the cool-stop temperature exceeds the targeted upper limit.
