Impact toughness tests were conducted on the welded samples with the Charpy V-notch prepared at the HAZ50/50 position. Figure  12  displays the HAZ50/50 toughness in comparison to the base metal toughness. The base metal toughness is approximately twice as high in the 0.04 pct C steels  vs.  the 0.06 pct C steels. However, the toughness at HAZ50/50 position is generally better in the 0.06 pct C steels achieving almost base metal toughness at − 20 °C and still performing rather well at − 40 °C. In contrast to that, a large difference between base metal and HAZ50/50 toughness is found for the 0.04 pct C steels. Particularly, the 4C10Nb steel shows poor HAZ50/50 toughness already at − 20 °C. This remarkable decay in toughness performance must be related to the substantially larger grain size present in the CGHAZ of the lower carbon steel (Figure  11 ). Fig. 12 Charpy toughness measurements in the mid-HAZ position (HAZ50/50) compared to the base metal (the columns represent the average value of three individual measurements)

In an approach to follow the evolution of grain growth in the CGHAZ, thermal cycles closely replicating the industrial GMAW cycle (Table  IV ) were simulated using a Gleeble device to various peak metal temperatures between 1250 °C and 1350 °C [Figure  13 (a)]. Inverse pole figures (IPF) obtained from EBSD analysis of such treated samples are displayed in Figure  13 (b). The 4C10Nb steel already shows a coarsened microstructure already at 1250 °C, while that of the 6C6Nb steel remained much finer under the same condition. As expected, the higher peak metal temperature of 1350 °C results in further coarsening of the microstructure with the 6C6Nb steel remaining generally finer-grained than the 4C10Nb steel. These observations suggest that grain growth proceeds gradually in the 6C6Nb steel with increasing peak metal temperature. The 4C10Nb steel, however, appears to experience a rather sudden and substantial grain growth already at temperatures below 1250 °C. Fig. 13 ( a ) Time–temperature cycle (black line) recorded during GMAW simulation in the Gleeble device and calculated cumulative Nb lattice diffusion distance (red line). ( b ) Inverse pole figure maps obtained by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis after simulated GMAW cycles (Color figure online)

The up-heating cycle passes the temperature range from 950 °C to 1350 °C within approximately 2 seconds corresponding to a heating rate of ~ 200 K/s. Calculating the diffusion range of niobium atoms over that time-temperature interval using lattice diffusion parameters ( D 0  = 0.83 cm 2 /s,  Q  = 266.5 kJ/mol [ 94 ] ) results in a value of less than 3  µ m [Figure  13 (a)]. The diffusion range over the entire austenite period is calculated to be around 8  µ m. These values are significantly smaller than the austenite grain sizes. Particularly, the austenite grain growth rate during up-heating must be very fast (Romualdi [ 89 ]  reported rates of up to 14  µ m/s at a much lower heating rate of 50 K/s) so that dissolving niobium atoms will be unable to reach a migrating boundary and accumulate there. Hence, a substantial contribution in impeding the austenite grain-boundary migration by niobium solute drag is not expected under the present conditions.

Charpy toughness data of these steels treated to three peak metal temperatures using the GMAW heat cycle simulation are congruent with the microstructural evolution. As seen in Figure  14 , toughness degradation proceeds gradually in the 6C6Nb with increasing peak metal temperature. That alloy also retains the highest toughness at 1350 °C. The 4C10Nb steel, on the contrary, experiences a sharp drop in toughness already at 1250 °C. Severe grain growth must have already occurred in the temperature range of 1000 °C to 1250 °C. The effects of a sudden reduction in pinning pressure due to quick dissolution of ultrafine NbC particles in combination with the fine-sized austenite grains are the potential reasons for that rapid grain growth. Fig. 14 Charpy toughness measurements after treating the steels with simulated GMAW cycles ( t 8/5  = 7 s) to various peak metal temperatures (the columns represent the average value of three individual measurements)

The general analysis of all previous observations allows the following conclusions regarding alloy design for weldable high-performance line pipe steels: A high niobium microalloy content provides an additional strengthening potential of 70 to 100 MPa in typical low-carbon line pipe steels. A lower carbon content achieves the higher base metal toughness but can be detrimental to CGHAZ toughness. The combination of a low-carbon content with a high niobium content requires careful assessment of the CGHAZ toughness performance. Redissolved niobium is apparently incapable of preventing rapid grain growth by solute drag on the austenite boundaries during the up-heating phase in a welding cycle. Titanium microalloying to a near-stoichiometric ratio with nitrogen is mandatory for controlling HAZ toughness performance; preferably TiN precipitation in the liquid phase is avoided in favor of finer-sized and more homogeneously distributed TiN and Ti, Nb (C, N) particles precipitating after full solidification. Molybdenum alloying has the potential of balancing base metal strength requirements and HAZ toughness performance.

sections.heading: Carburizing Treatments on Gear Steels
paragraphs: Case carburizing steels are widely used in applications where high near-surface hardness is required in combination with good core toughness as well as high strength and fatigue resistance. [ 95 ]  These steels have been the material of choice for several decades for manufacturing components like gears, shafts, or bearings. The thermomechanical processing of respective components involves a complex sequence of individual forming, machining, and heat treatment operations including the final case carburizing treatment (Figure  15 ). In that final treatment, the component is heated to a temperature in the austenite range in the presence of a carbon containing gas atmosphere. Traditional industrial processes limit this temperature to 950 °C, while high-temperature carburizing up to 1050 °C is in demand as it allows significantly shorter treatment times. [ 95 ,  96 ,  97 – 98 ]  The holding time at carburizing temperature covers a wide range of up to 100 hours depending on the required depth of the carburizing layer. It is important that during such long holding time the austenite grain structure is not excessively coarsening which would result in a loss of properties relevant to component performance. Established industry standards limit the share of grains having size ASTM 5 to maximum 10 pct, while grain sizes coarser than ASTM 5 are generally not permitted. For optimum component performance, the average grain size should be moderately fine (ASTM 7-8) with a homogeneous size distribution. [ 95 ]  A fraction of individual large or extremely fine grains is not only detrimental to relevant properties but can also develop considerable residual stresses upon quenching, causing severe shape distortion of the component. [ 95 ,  96 – 97 ]  The final grain size distribution in steels subjected to a carburizing treatment is decisively influenced by all prior operations. These include hot and cold forming as well as annealing treatments in the ferrite and austenite temperature range. Fig. 15 Typical processing sequences for manufacturing of case carburized components and commonly used time–temperature schedules for intermediate heat treatments

sections.heading: Microalloying Concepts for Coarsening Resistance During Carburizing
paragraphs: Standard steel-making practices for forging steels are based on electric arc furnace (EAF) melting and aluminum deoxidation. The typical contents of 80 to 150 ppm nitrogen and 200 to 500 ppm aluminum result in the precipitation of AlN particles in the finished steel. These principally have the potential to restrict austenite grain coarsening during carburizing treatments, keeping in mind that the species dissolves above 950 °C. The ideal aluminum-to-nitrogen ratio of 1.92:1 mass pct providing the best particle stability is, however, difficult to maintain under industrial production circumstances. [ 99 , 100 ]  Principally, AlN particles effectively control grain coarsening at lower carburizing temperature. However, AlN is an anisotropic ionic compound having a hexagonal B4 (wurtzite) lattice structure that grows to a prismatic morphology along preferred planes in the bcc host lattice. When such elongated particles are present in the matrix and the interfacial energy in one grain is smaller than that in the adjacent one, the boundary between both grains is induced to migrate. This effect, also designated as “inverse pinning,” can be detrimental to grain size control. [ 101 ]

Consequently, high-temperature carburizing requires a modification of the alloy in a way to provide particle with superior temperature stability to prevent excessive grain coarsening. Niobium and titanium are in this respect the most obvious microalloys due to the low solubility of their carbides and nitrides at the relevant austenite temperatures. The addition of niobium is limited to around 0.05 mass pct since higher amounts cannot be brought into solution during soaking in the typical medium carbon steels. The limit for titanium additions should be even lower considering the high residual nitrogen level in EAF-generated steel bearing the risk of forming coarse cube-shaped particles in the last solidifying liquid phase. [ 102 ]  These particles have no significant contribution to austenite grain size control and, on the other hand, are harmful regarding toughness and fatigue performance.

The use of titanium and niobium microalloying for controlling the austenite grain size during carburizing treatments of forging steels has been initially investigated by Huchtemann and Schüler. [ 100 ]  Single microalloying of titanium to the standard gear steel 16MnCrS5 (AISI 5115) showed a clear improvement of the coarse grain limit temperature to around 1150 °C  vs . 990 °C for the Ti-free steel based on a reference carburizing treatment. The maximum coarsening resistance was achieved for a Ti:N ratio clearly below the stoichiometric ratio of 3.4:1 (in mass pct). Microalloying of niobium (0.06 mass pct) in Ti-free steel resulted in coarse grain limit temperatures of 1000 °C to 1150 °C. This relatively wide range originates from the intermediate heat treatment conditions having a decisive impact on the niobium particle distribution (number density and spatial distribution) in the steel. The combination of niobium (0.05 to 0.07 mass pct) with small additions of titanium (up to 0.01 mass pct) provided the best resistance against grain coarsening for reference carburizing treatments even up to 1230 °C (Figure  16 ). For the combined Nb + Ti microalloying concept, the influence caused by the intermediate heat treatment is much reduced. This implies that a population of temperature-stable Nb, Ti (C, N) particles must have already formed during the initial hot working stage. The anti-coarsening effect of such particles principally corresponds to what has already been described earlier in this paper regarding grain size control in the CGHAZ during welding. A detailed analysis of combined niobium and titanium additions considering solubility, precipitate distribution, and particle coarsening in a SAE 8620 steel by Alogab  et al . [ 103 ]  confirmed that Ti-modified steels with approximately 0.06 mass pct Nb have the best potential in providing optimum resistance to grain growth at higher carburizing temperatures. Fig. 16 Effect of the Ti, Nb, and combined Ti–Nb microalloy content on the temperature of initial austenite grain coarsening for a reference holding time applied to steel 16MnCrS5 (adapted from Mohrbacher [ 106 ] )

Leap and Brown [ 104 ]  claimed that grain coarsening is largely independent of the pre-processing history in steels containing niobium and aluminum, since the presence of Nb (C, N) in the microstructure compensates for the comparatively low thermodynamic stability of AIN. However, the evolution of the matrix microstructure before austenitizing does have a substantial effect on grain coarsening resistance when a steel containing any combination of carbide and nitride forming elements is processed to contain a large volume fraction of fine precipitates. Hence, developing appropriate precursor microstructures during pre-processing and eliminating cold work from the microstructure before austenitizing are important prerequisites when carburizing cold-forged steels. This approach was confirmed by Klenke  et al . [ 105 ]  on a 20NiMoCr6 − 5 + Nb steel after various degrees of cold forming in the range of 5 to 50 pct followed by recrystallization annealing. The steel was resistant against grain coarsening for at least 4 hours isothermal holding at a carburizing temperature of 1050 °C. As compared to a lower carburizing temperature of 990 °C, only a moderate uniform increase of average grain size was observed at 1050 °C. Other examples of microalloy concepts for preventing excessive austenite grain coarsening during high-temperature carburizing of large gear components were given by Tobie  et al . [ 95 ]

sections.heading: Effect of Intermediate Heat Treatments on Microalloy Precipitates
paragraphs: The particle population must be carefully adjusted already early in the processing sequence to ultimately provide efficient grain-boundary pinning in the final carburizing treatment. The general aim is to maximize the particle count and to achieve a homogenous distribution as well as sufficient thermodynamic stability of these particles at the intended carburizing temperature.

Niobium that has been redissolved by a soaking treatment does not easily re-precipitate in austenite. This is due to the large mismatch (~ 25 pct) between the NbC and austenite lattice parameters, respectively. Strain-induced NbC precipitation, however, occurs to some degree when deforming austenite in the temperature range of 900 °C to 930 °C. The remaining solute niobium is retained in supersaturation especially when applying accelerated cooling after hot deformation. It is then available for precipitation during subsequent heat treatments resulting in copious and fine-sized secondary precipitates providing a high Zener pinning pressure on grain boundaries. [ 107 ]

The particle population established in the steel matrix before carburizing is expected to progressively coarsen over the duration of the treatment. Interfacial energy acts as the primary driving force promoting precipitate coarsening (Ostwald ripening), as the system reduces its total energy by eliminating the high-curvature interfaces adhering to smaller-sized particles. Higher interfacial energy increases the rate of coarsening, while lower energy provides better thermal stability. Solute niobium left in the matrix due to incomplete precipitation during prior treatments is readily available to feed the growth of existing particles. In fully precipitated condition, however, part of the existing smaller precipitates must first dissolve to enable particle coarsening. The amount of niobium that can redissolve is controlled by the solubility product [Figure  17 (a)]. Niobium must be microalloyed in excess to the solubility at the targeted carburizing temperature. Therefore, it must be considered that part of the niobium content might form an epitaxial layer on TiN particles [ 97 ]  and is thus inactive. Multi-component microalloy compounds due to their smaller solubility product as compared to binary carbides have a better resilience against particle coarsening at the applied holding temperature. When a particle population evolves into fewer but larger particles over time by Ostwald ripening, the Zener pinning pressure gradually decreases. The diffusion range of the microalloy atoms is a limiting factor to particle growth. The diffusion range of niobium is estimated to be less than 10  µ m even for very long treatment time at conventional carburizing temperatures (< 950 °C). High-temperature carburizing conditions may extend the diffusion range up to 30  µ m. Wey  et al . [ 108 ]  modeled and experimentally verified the particle growth rates of various transition metal carbide species in austenite. Niobium carbide was found to have a very low growth rate of approximately 10 −10 µ m 3 /s at 900 °C and 10 −9 µ m 3 /s at 1000 °C. Based on these growth rates, the precipitate size evolution of niobium carbide was calculated for two starting particle sizes [Figure  17 (b)]. It appears that a starting particle of around 20 nm is quite ideal for high carburizing temperatures. This particle size and thus the Zener pinning pressure remain stable during the early treatment phase that is most sensitive to rapid or even abnormal grain growth. An average starting particle size of 20 nm can be expected after an intermediate soft annealing treatment [Figure  18 (a)]. Ultrafine-sized NbC particles (~ 5 nm) will grow rather quickly during the early treatment stage even at low carburizing temperature. Over a longer treatment period, particle sizes assimilate and grow to diameters in the range of 30 to 70 nm. Fig. 17 ( a ) Solubility limit of NbC, [ 62 ]  Nb (C, N), [ 110 ]  and mixed Nb–Ti (C, N) [ 85 ]  in austenite (C: 0.2 mass pct, N: 100 mass ppm) and operating range for Nb-microalloyed carburizing steel. ( b ) Calculated coarsening of NbC particles in function of annealing time and temperature for two starting sizes using the approach of Wey  et al . [ 108 ]  and duration of typical carburizing treatments Fig. 18 ( a ) Progress of microalloy precipitation from supersaturated solution in a 18CrNiMo7-6 steel (290 ppm Al, 120 ppm N, 310 ppm Nb, 30 ppm Ti) during soft annealing at 680 °C and ( b ) evolution of the Zener pinning pressure during subsequent carburizing at 1050 °C for various soft annealing conditions (based on calculations by Konovalov [ 111 ] )

Enloe  et al . [ 90 ]  demonstrated that molybdenum has the potential of significantly reducing the coarsening rate of NbC particles. Various mechanisms were held responsible for this effect. Molybdenum was assumed reducing the frequency factor for niobium diffusion, thus slowing down the flux of solute niobium atoms away from a dissolving smaller particle. In addition, molybdenum segregating at the particle–matrix interface should further enhance this effect. The segregation of molybdenum to the particle–matrix interface of TiC precipitates and the resulting impediment of particle growth was demonstrated by Seol  et al . [ 109 ]  This mechanism identically applies to NbC precipitates.

A frequently used intermediate heat treatment after forging is the so-called FP annealing to obtain a normalized ferritic–pearlitic microstructure (Figure  15 ). The forged component is re-austenitized and held in austenite for about 2 hours followed by cooling to below  A c1  temperature resulting in a normalized grain structure. Subsequent extended holding at a temperature close to  A c1  spheroidizes the newly formed pearlite. Niobium, when added to such a steel, precipitates nearly completely during up-heating to austenitizing temperature. Slow heating rates in the intercritical temperature range can lead to particle coarsening to some degree and more severely for titanium than for niobium carbides. Particle coarsening is promoted by partial redissolution of microalloy carbides in the intercritical temperature range and particularly by increased diffusional range above the Curie temperature as discussed earlier in this paper. [ 17 ]  Alternatively, soft annealing below  A c1  temperature can be practiced resulting in a recrystallized microstructure, spheroidization of pearlite and complete niobium precipitation to fine particles sizes. Yet, the ferrite grain size might be coarser and less homogenous as compared to FP annealing. Excessive microalloy particle coarsening is not expected during soft annealing even if the forged component is held for an extended period at temperature.

Konovalov  et al . [ 111 ]  and Rudnizki  et al . [ 112 ]  described a sophisticated thermodynamic simulation approach with the aim of identifying robust processing chains that result in stable control of fine austenite grain sizes during the high-temperature carburization. An example of such a simulation shows the evolution of the Zener pinning pressure provided by microalloy particles at intermediate and final heat treatment stages using a 18CrNiMo7-6 gear steel (Figure  18 ). Starting from a condition of fully dissolved microalloys by soaking the steel at 1220 °C and subsequent fast cooling, microalloy particles precipitate during soft annealing at 680 °C. These particles grow to an experimentally verified average size of around 17 nm within 8 hours, while precipitation is completed after around 20 hours. Extended holding of up to 80 hours does not cause measurable further particle coarsening, which was also experimentally verified. Accordingly, the initial Zener pinning pressure at the start of a subsequent carburizing treatment at 1050 °C is maximized after an intermediate treatment at 680 °C for 20 hours. During the carburizing treatment, particle coarsening occurs and the Zener pinning pressure gradually decreases over time. Since shorter intermediate holding periods at 680 °C result in incomplete microalloy precipitation, the Zener pinning pressure at the start of the carburizing treatment is lower. In that case, precipitation of the residual solute microalloys proceeds during the early carburizing phase after which the initial differences in the Zener pinning pressure equalize out. The progressing particle coarsening [Figure  17 (b)] continuously reduces the Zener pinning pressure over time resulting in general austenite grain growth. It is however important to establish a sufficiently high Zener pinning pressure during the early carburizing stage for suppressing abnormal grain growth especially when starting from a fine grain size providing a large driving force for growth. [ 112 ]

The aim of establishing a homogeneously distributed particle population can be spoiled by segregation phenomena occurring during solidification of the cast steel as was described by Davis and Strangwood. [ 113 ]  Concentration variations due to segregation cannot be fully leveled out during later heat treatments. [ 114 ]  The resulting precipitate-rich zones produce very fine austenite grain sizes, while coarser grain sizes appear in precipitate-depleted areas. [ 98 ]  Under high-temperature carburizing conditions, the presence of such segregation zones promotes the conditions for abnormal growth. Furthermore, quenching an austenite microstructure containing a large span of grain sizes results in an inhomogeneous martensite transformation, [ 95 , 115 , 116 ]  causing the generation of significant residual stresses. The correction of such induced shape distortion involves undesirable and costly hard machining of the finished component.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This paper reviewed fundamental characteristics of microalloying elements regarding their effects on recovery, recrystallization, phase transformation, and grain growth. Relevant properties are the atom size, the solubility, and temperature stability of related carbides or nitrides, the tendency of segregating at grain boundaries, dislocations, and point defects, as well as the diffusivity. The most important interactions and observations can be summarized as follows: Annealing treatments in the ferrite phase below  A r1  temperature are strongly influenced by niobium and molybdenum in solute condition. Niobium atoms have a larger binding energy to grain boundaries and dislocations than molybdenum atoms. However, molybdenum is soluble in ferrite to a considerably larger content than niobium. At annealing temperatures above  A r1 , niobium efficiently precipitates as NbC in ferrite, thus, gradually losing its solute drag effect and building up particle pinning potential. The combined addition of niobium and molybdenum provides a synergy between solute drag and particle pinning at such higher annealing temperatures. When annealing above the Curie temperature (~ 770 °C), the diffusivity of microalloying elements sharply increases and solute drag effects in paramagnetic ferrite weaken considerably. In the intercritical temperature range, microalloy carbides can redissolve in the ferrite phase while remaining stable in the coexisting austenite phase. This is promoted by carbon depletion and enrichment of the coexisting ferrite and austenite, respectively. The enhanced microalloy diffusivity above the Curie temperature simultaneously promotes particle coarsening. The resulting loss in particle pinning pressure is largest for vanadium and least for niobium. Complex microalloy particles involving are more resilient against the redissolution and coarsening mechanism. Passing through the intercritical temperature range under slow heating rates is particularly detrimental in this respect. The delay of ferrite recrystallization supported by niobium and molybdenum far into the intercritical temperature range promotes strong interaction with austenite transformation resulting in a very fine-grained initial austenite microstructure. The simultaneously forming niobium precipitates are capable of preserving this fine-grained austenite microstructure up to the temperature of NbC dissolution. The fine-grained austenite exerts a high driving force for grain growth and can result in quick coarsening when NbC particles start redissolving at increasing austenite temperature. Under unfavorable circumstances, this can induce abnormal grain growth. Stabilization of such particles by a complex composition with Ti, N, and eventually Mo as well as an increased carbon content in the steel can retard particle dissolution and prevent abnormal grain growth. Solute niobium and molybdenum have the potency of retarding grain growth at high austenite temperatures when segregating at the austenite grain boundary and exerting solute drag. Upon cooling from the austenite peak temperature, grain-boundary enrichment of microalloys is efficiently assisted by non-equilibrium segregation and results in a lower transformation temperature. Microalloying elements, and particularly titanium and niobium, have a tendency for segregating during solidification related to the low solubility of these elements in the solidifying phase. This can lead to micro- and macro-segregation zones with microalloy enrichment considerably above the nominal addition level. Consequently, recrystallization and growth retarding effects by microalloying elements can be inhomogeneous across the microstructure contributing to inhomogeneous grain size distribution after heat treatments.

The implementation of these insights in industrially produced steels has enabled considerable improvements in terms of product properties and processing efficiency. Several examples were demonstrated in this paper covering strip, plate, and forging products.
